strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP: repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate estimates of generalization to unseen subjects and text.

Investigates two established architectures across EEG/ZuCo and fMRI/Narratives, with multiple splitting strategies, additional held-out evaluation, and input-shuffling controls. Table 6 reports lower scores under the proposed split even without teacher forcing, supporting a narrower empirical contribution.

Separating both subject and stimulus identities is a sensible evaluation target for joint generalization. The paper's contribution could be valuable as a methodological audit without introducing a new decoding architecture.
weaknesses: The headline benchmark uses teacher forcing. Table 6 identifies the scores reused in Tables 3–5 as teacher-forced results, so the proposed 'fair benchmark' does not measure free-running generation. The additional-test and shuffled-input controls are not reported without teacher forcing; access to ground-truth prefixes therefore remains an alternative explanation for apparent independence from brain signals. Appendix E partially addresses this issue, but the principal benchmark and controls need evaluation without ground-truth prefixes.

The published splitting algorithms do not enforce their claimed guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, excludes held-out subjects when adding edges but does not exclude held-out text nodes. Algorithm 2, line 33, excludes held-out stories but not held-out subjects. These expansion steps can reintroduce overlap, contrary to Equations 13–14. The pseudocode, implementation, and actual split assignments must be reconciled before the zero-leakage claim is reproducible.

The comparisons do not adequately separate leakage effects from changes in data quantity and distribution. Retained/discarded sample counts and the construction, size, and subject/story composition of the additional test set are missing. An 80:10:10 ratio does not establish comparable training resources or test difficulty. No implementation or split manifests are linked, and repeated-seed uncertainty is reported for leakage rates rather than decoding performance. These omissions are particularly consequential for subject-level evaluation on the small ZuCo dataset.

The interpretation overreaches. Subject overlap invalidates claims about unseen-subject generalization, but does not inherently invalidate evaluation for previously observed subjects. Likewise, transfer across subjects on familiar stimuli differs from generating unseen text. Declaring all existing protocols 'wrong' requires examining their intended evaluation targets. Moreover, decreasing validation reconstruction loss in Section 5.2 does not demonstrate degrading encoder representations, and improving test scores with longer training does not itself establish leakage.

The formal analysis contains substantive errors. Equations 6–7 universally quantify over training examples, thereby failing to characterize leakage affecting only some examples. Equation 17 counts overlapping signal instances rather than shared subject identities, leaving the reported nonzero rates for disjoint sample splits unexplained. Appendix D's universal claim that samples must be discarded also lacks a connectivity assumption: disconnected subject–stimulus components can be assigned to different splits without discarding data.

Quantitative reporting needs verification. Table 3 labels 40.65 as ROUGE-1 F for Narratives/method (a), whereas Table 7 labels that value recall and reports F=44.83. Appendix E describes EEG method (d) as having no text leakage despite Tables 1–2 reporting leakage. Together with the evaluation and algorithmic issues, these inconsistencies prevent a sound Findings recommendation; corrected protocols and reruns constitute a plausible next-cycle revision.
